title: A/B testing fundamentals | How LLMs are trained and served
objectives: Design an experiment end to end and catch validity threats. Understand the LLM lifecycle from pretraining to inference. Checkpoint 1 on Day 7.
exercise: Write a one-page experiment design doc for a real feature from your current fintech job, including sizing and an SRM check.
resources: Kohavi, Tang & Xu, Ch. 3 (Twyman's law) and Ch. 21 (SRM and trust guardrails)
Fabijan et al., Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch, KDD 2019 (exp-platform.com)

units.title: Experiment design checklist
units.concepts: Hypothesis, unit, metrics, sizing, duration, analysis plan

units.title: Novelty, Twyman & guardrails
units.concepts: Novelty/primacy effects, Twyman's law, guardrail metrics

cards.q: Put the experiment design steps in order.
Why write the analysis plan before launch?
choices: To avoid choosing metrics, segments or stopping rules after seeing the data (p-hacking)

cards.q: A guardrail metric is…
choices: A metric that must not degrade beyond a threshold even if the primary metric wins (e.g. latency, payment failures)
A metric used to size the test
A metric only checked after launch

cards.q: Why run experiments in whole-week multiples?
choices: To cover day-of-week cycles so weekday/weekend behaviour is balanced

cards.q: Audit this plan: 'Randomise by session. Primary metric: revenue per user. Check results daily and stop as soon as p < 0.05. Then look at 15 segments to find where it works.'
cards.answer: 1) Session randomisation means the same user sees both variants (contamination), and the analysis unit (user) ≠ the randomisation unit. 2) Daily peeking with stop-on-significance inflates the false-positive rate; fix the duration or use a sequential test. 3) Post-hoc 15 segments is a multiple-testing problem; pre-register segments or correct. 4) No guardrails, no sizing, no SRM check. 5) Revenue is heavy-tailed; plan for capping/CUPED.
rubric: Session vs user randomisation / unit mismatch

cards.q: You randomise by city but analyse per order. What goes wrong with naive SEs?
cards.answer: Orders within a city share shocks (weather, supply, promos), so they're correlated. The effective sample size is closer to the number of cities than the number of orders. Naive i.i.d. SEs are far too small, which gives overconfident CIs and false positives. Use cluster-robust SEs, analyse at city level, or use the delta method on city-level ratios.
rubric: Naive SE too small → false positives
Fix: cluster-robust SE / aggregate / delta method

cards.q: Design effect = 1 + (m − 1)·ICC. With 100 orders per cluster and ICC = 0.05, what is the design effect? (2 dp)
cards.explain: The variance is ~6× the naive estimate, so the effective sample size is ~1/6 of the order count.

cards.q: Why randomise by user rather than by page view?
choices: Consistent experience per user and independent units; page views from one user are correlated and contaminated

cards.q: When do you need cluster (e.g. city or geo) randomisation?
choices: When treating one unit affects others' outcomes (interference/network effects)

cards.q: A test randomised 40 cities. Which statement is true?
choices: Power is limited mostly by 40 clusters, however many orders you have
Millions of orders guarantee high power
You can ignore clustering if n_orders > 1M

cards.q: A 50/50 test shows 821,588 vs 815,482 users. Is that a problem?
choices: Yes: chi-square p < 1/500k; it's a Sample Ratio Mismatch
cards.explain: With large n, tiny relative gaps are highly significant.

cards.q: Compute the chi-square SRM statistic for 821,588 vs 815,482 with an expected 50/50 split. (1 dp)
Which is a common cause of SRM?
choices: Treatment changes who gets logged (redirect drops, bot filtering, crashes before logging, trigger conditions)

cards.q: You detect SRM. What should you do?
choices: Treat the results as untrustworthy and find the cause before analysing
Re-weight the arms and report the result
Ignore it if p < 0.05 on the metric
Drop the larger arm's extra users at random
cards.explain: Fabijan et al. (KDD 2019) catalogue the causes of SRM and treat it as a sign that results can't be trusted until the cause is explained.

cards.q: Which statistical test is the standard SRM check?
choices: Chi-square goodness-of-fit against the designed split

cards.q: A UI test shows +8% sessions in week 1. Name two reasons to distrust it.
cards.answer: Novelty effect: curiosity spikes that decay. Twyman's law: a surprisingly large effect is usually a bug, so check logging, SRM and bots. Week 1 alone doesn't cover the weekly cycle or a long-term trend. More sessions can even signal confusion (users can't complete the task). It's also a proxy, so check the downstream metric.
rubric: Twyman's law / instrumentation or SRM bug

cards.q: Twyman's law says…
choices: Any figure that looks interesting or different is usually wrong

cards.q: Novelty vs primacy effect?
choices: Novelty: early lift that fades; primacy: early dip (change aversion) that recovers
Novelty affects only new users; primacy only bots
Primacy is a lift that grows

cards.q: How can you detect a novelty effect?
choices: Plot the treatment effect by day since first exposure, and compare new vs returning users

cards.q: Good guardrail for a checkout redesign at a payments company?
What does next-token prediction optimise, and why does it produce general capabilities?
cards.answer: It minimises cross-entropy, i.e. it maximises the log-likelihood of the next token given the context. To predict diverse internet-scale text well, the model must implicitly learn syntax, facts, world regularities and reasoning patterns. Those internal representations transfer to many tasks.
rubric: Cross-entropy / log-likelihood of the next token
Good prediction requires modelling knowledge and structure

cards.q: Scaling laws describe…
choices: Loss falling as a smooth power law in parameters, data and compute

cards.q: Chinchilla's key finding on compute-optimal training?
choices: Scale parameters and training tokens roughly in proportion (~20 tokens/param)
Train smaller models for longer is always worse

cards.q: Average cross-entropy is 2.3026 nats per token. What is the perplexity?
A raw pretrained (base) model asked a question typically…
choices: Continues the text plausibly, not necessarily answering helpfully
cards.explain: Post-training turns it into an assistant.

cards.q: How does DPO differ from RLHF with PPO?
choices: No separate reward model or RL loop: it optimises the policy directly on preference pairs

cards.q: Order a typical LLM training pipeline.
items: Optional RL with verifiable rewards for reasoning

cards.q: In RLHF, why add a KL penalty to the reference model?
choices: To stop the policy drifting into reward-model exploits (reward hacking) and degenerate text

cards.q: SFT data consists of…
What characterises a 'reasoning model'?
choices: Trained (often via RL on verifiable tasks) to think in long chains before answering, trading test-time compute for accuracy

cards.q: Which setting makes outputs more deterministic: temperature 0.2 or 1.0?
cards.explain: Logits are divided by T; a low T sharpens the distribution.

cards.q: Top-p (nucleus) sampling…
choices: Samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability ≥ p
Picks the token with probability p

cards.q: Recommended setting for extracting fields into JSON?
choices: Low temperature (≈0) plus a schema-constrained output

cards.q: Is temperature 0 always perfectly reproducible via a hosted API?
choices: Not guaranteed: batching and floating-point non-determinism can change outputs

cards.q: As temperature → 0, sampling approaches…
Give two reasons a fintech might choose an open-weight model over an API.
cards.answer: Data residency/privacy: regulated customer data can't leave its infrastructure. Control: pinned versions with no silent deprecation, plus full fine-tuning freedom. Cost at high volume. Latency/on-prem deployment. Auditability for regulators.
rubric: Any two of: data privacy/residency, version control, fine-tuning freedom, cost at scale, latency/on-prem, auditability

cards.q: First step when choosing between three candidate models for a task?
choices: Build a task-specific eval set and compare quality, cost and latency on it
Pick the top public leaderboard model

cards.q: Quantising weights from 16-bit to 4-bit typically…
choices: Cuts weight memory ~4× and often speeds memory-bound decoding (kernel-dependent), with a small quality loss

cards.q: Why isn't 'just use the biggest context window' always right?
choices: Cost and latency grow with tokens, and models can miss information buried mid-context
Small contexts are always more accurate

cards.q: The cost/latency/quality triangle means…
choices: Improving one usually costs another; pick the point your product needs
All three improve together with bigger models
Latency is irrelevant for batch jobs only
